title: TA7-14025
frame:
Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX (the claimant) alleges to be a citizen of the People's Republic of China. He claims to have a well-founded fear of persecution at the hands of the Communist regime and in particular, the Public Security Bureau, by reason of his identity as a practicing Christian who attended an unregistered house church in China. In addition, he claims to be a person in need of protection because he would be subjected personally to a risk to his life or to a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment or to a danger of torture in the People's Republic of China. He claims refugee protection pursuant to section 96 and subsection 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act.1 ALLEGATIONS:
The claimant alleges that he was born in Guangzhou City, Guangdong province, China. He alleges that in XXXXX 2006 his mother was diagnosed with XXXXX cancer.

In XXXXX 2006, the claimant's friend XXXXX XXXXX visited him and during the visit they discussed the claimant's mother's poor health. Mr. XXXXX confided in the claimant that he was a Christian who attended an unregistered house church in China. Mr. XXXXX began to teach the claimant about Christianity and he invited the claimant to join his unregistered house church.
On XXXXX XXXXX, 2006, the claimant attended Mr. XXXXX the house church for the first time. In XXXXX 2006, the claimant's mother received news from her doctor that her health had greatly improved.
On XXXXX XXXXX, 2007, the claimant was baptized at the unregistered house church.

On XXXXX XXXXX, 2007, during a house church service one of the look-outs advised the participants that the Public Security Bureau was approaching the house. The claimant escaped the house and went to his friend's home to hide.

While in hiding, the claimant learned that the Public Security Bureau had gone to his home on XXXXX XXXXX and had searched his home and questioned his family about his whereabouts. The Public Security Bureau advised his family that they had arrested four other house church members and that they had evidence against the claimant.

The claimant decided that he could not safely remain in China and contracted the services of a smuggler to assist him to leave China and to travel to Canada. The claimant arrived in Canada on XXXXX XXXXX, 2007 and on October 17, 2007, the claimant made a claim for refugee protection in Canada. DETERMINATION:
The Panel has found, on a balance of probabilities that the claimant's testimony is not credible with respect to his identity as a national of the People's Republic of China for reasons that follow.

Furthermore, on the basis that the Panel cannot determine the claimant's identity, the Panel is unable to determine the identity of the claimant as a national of the People's Republic of China. Accordingly the Panel is unable to determine that the claimant is a Convention refugee or that he is a person in need of protection. ANALYSIS: The Issue of Missing Documents and the Subsequent Adjournment to Allow the Claimant to provide the Documents

The hearing was held over two sittings, on January 19, 2010 and on April 28, 2010. The hearing was adjourned on January 19, 2010 to allow the claimant the opportunity to provide personal identity documents to the Panel.

The claimant filed his claim for refugee protection on October 19, 2007, over two years before the first sitting of his hearing on January 19, 2010. The claimant was represented by an Immigration consultant when he filed his application for refugee protection with Citizenship and Immigration Canada2 and was later represented by qualified, experienced Counsel when he completed and signed his Personal Information Form on December 24, 20073 and he was also represented by the same Counsel at the hearing.

When the claimant arrived in Canada he had no identity documents. He alleges that he traveled to Canada with a non-genuine Singapore passport which had been arranged by the smuggler. He indicated that he no longer had the Singapore passport because he gave the passport back to the smuggler. The claimant indicated that he did not have a Resident Identity Card because it had been seized by the Chinese postal authorities when his father had previously attempted to mail it to him.

In his oral testimony, the claimant initially stated that his parents attempted to mail the Resident Identity card to him from China in August 2008. He then changed his testimony and stated that his parents attempted to mail the document in September 2008. When asked to describe how the document was seized, the claimant stated that his parents were asked by the postal official, "what are you sending?" and his parents told the postal official that their son, the claimant, is in Canada and that they were sending "something useful" to him because the Canadian government needs the Resident Identity card. When given the opportunity to explain why his parents would tell the postal official that his Resident Identity card was in the package and that it was being mailed for use by the Canadian government, the claimant responded that his parents were "straight forward, honest people". Although the claimant's parents may well be honest people, the Panel rejects this explanation as unreasonable and implausible given that the claimant's parents were aware that their son was in danger and was living in Canada because of his pursuit by the Public Security Bureau and it is implausible that they would voluntarily admit to a Chinese official that they were sending the Resident Identity document to their son. The Panel furthermore draws a negative inference in regard to credibility and to the claimant's identity as a Chinese national.

The Panel is guided in making this finding of implausibility by legal jurisprudence as stated in the decision of Justice Barnes in Chen4 who cautions the Panel when making findings of implausibility to base the assessment on the actual testimony of the claimant and not what the Panel thinks a claimant would have said had he been asked. Having taken this caution into consideration, and having given the claimant the opportunity to explain why his parents would tell the post office official that the Canadian government needs the claimant's Resident Identity card knowing that their son was wanted by the Public Security Bureau, the Panel finds the explanation given to be implausible. The claimant allegedly fled to Canada to seek protection from the Public Security Bureau and he testified that his parents were aware both of the circumstances leading to his departure for Canada and also his application for refugee protection in Canada. For these reasons, and in the absence of any reasonable explanation as to why his parents would disclose not only his Resident Identity card but also the reason for its being sent to Canada to postal authorities who are Chinese government officials, the Panel draws a negative inference in regard to credibility. Furthermore the testimony offered by the claimant contradicts the seizure notice provided in support of the allegation that the document was seized. The claimant testified that the postal official became aware of the Resident Identity card by his father volunteering the information when asked, however the seizure notice states that the Resident Identity card was discovered "when Bureau officer Dong Kui Liu sorted out the package [sic]... the Resident Identity card was discovered and because it is a contraband item, it could not be mailed out".5 Counsel requested that the interpreter assisting at the hearing review the document to confirm the wording and to advise the Panel. The interpreter confirmed that the written Seizure notice indicated that the notice said that the Resident Identity card was discovered when the postal worker was checking the mail, therefore the Notice from the Postal Bureau clearly indicates that the Resident Identity Card was discovered while the mail was being sorted and makes no mention of the claimant's father disclosing this information. The Panel draws a negative inference in regard to credibility and the claimant's identity as a national of China given the contradiction between his oral testimony and the corroborating evidence he provided from the Chinese Postal Bureau.

When the claimant attended the first sitting of his hearing in January 2010 he presented the Panel with only one identity document, his Chinese family household registry record.6 As stated above, the claimant stated that his Chinese Resident Identity Card had been confiscated by the Chinese postal officials and provided a notice from the Chinese post office in support of this claim which states that his Resident Identity Card was seized after the post office, having "sorted out the package" to be mailed found it contained a Resident Identity Card.7

The Panel asked the claimant if he had been aware that his personal identity as a national of the People's Republic of China would be an issue in his claim prior to the hearing, and the claimant responded in the affirmative. When asked the direct question of "Where is your birth certificate?", the claimant initially responded that he did not have a birth certificate. He then changed this testimony and said that both his genuine original birth certificate and genuine original Chinese passport are in China with his parents. The Panel draws a negative inference in regard to credibility given the claimant's changing testimony regarding whether or not he has a birth certificate and given the claimant's inconsistent internal evidence regarding a straight forward question.

The claimant was reminded that the Immigration and Refugee Board screening form,8 which is sent out to both the claimant and Counsel on May 15, 2009, provided instructions to his Counsel and the claimant, stating he must provide his hukou (Chinese household registry), his resident identity card and his passport to the Panel. The claimant responded that he had been aware that his passport was required for the hearing but that he ignored these instructions because of his Resident Identity Card being previously confiscated. The Panel rejects the claimant's explanations regarding the absence of his personal identity documents, given that he was aware prior to the hearing that his personal identity would be an issue in his claim, especially in the absence of his Chinese Resident Identity Card, and because he was represented by qualified, experienced Counsel.

The claimant stated that he had his Chinese family household registry record for the hearing because his parents had mailed it to him, but they had not sent him his genuine original birth certificate and genuine original Chinese passport. When asked by the Panel why he failed to provide the documents to the Panel when he provided his Chinese family household registry, the claimant initially stated that his Counsel did not tell him that he needed to bring his Chinese birth certificate to the hearing and then changed his earlier testimony and stated that his Counsel did not advise him that his personal identity would be an issue in his claim. The Panel draws a negative inference in regard to credibility given the claimant's changing testimony regarding whether or not he was aware that his personal identity would be an important element of his claim, given his earlier testimony in which he stated he was aware of the issue of identity from the Immigration and Refugee Board screening form in May 2009 and his later testimony that his Counsel did not make him aware that identity would be an issue.

During his oral testimony when asked why he did not provide the Panel with his genuine original passport, the claimant stated that because previously his Resident Identity Card had been confiscated in the mail by the Chinese postal authorities, he did not want to risk having his passport mailed to Canada. The Panel then asked him why he had felt comfortable having his Chinese household registry mailed to him and the claimant said that this was because his parents had said that they would mail the household registry because "it is not as important as a passport". Later, the claimant stated that he did not have his passport sent to him because the interpreter who assisted him in the completion of his forms advised him that he needed his resident identity card, but not his birth certificate or passport for his hearing. The Panel draws a negative inference in regard to credibility given the claimant's changing testimony regarding why he failed to provide his Chinese passport to the Panel.

The claimant was asked why he failed to mention the existence of both his birth certificate and passport in his Personal Information Form, where it asks "What other identity documents do you have or could you obtain"?9 In this section, the claimant had indicated that both his resident identity card and his household registration document were in China but could be provided, but he failed to identify any other available documents. The claimant responded that he was "not told" that he needed to include this information in his Personal Information Form. The Panel rejects this explanation as nonsensical and draws a negative inference in regard to credibility, given that question twenty-two of the Personal Information Form clearly directs claimants to provide this information.

The claimant was then asked why when he completed his Personal Information Form on December 24, 2007 he had stated that he had used a Singapore passport but that he had no other passport,10 given that during his oral t testimony he stated that he had an original genuine Chinese passport in China. He was asked why this information was originally omitted from his Personal Information Form and the word "none" was indicated under the section regarding passports, but later during the first sitting of the hearing, he amended the form to indicate that he had an original genuine Chinese passport in China, but he was unable to specify the serial number, date of issue or date of expiry.11 The claimant speculated that the omission of his Chinese passport from his Personal Information Form was caused by the person who completed form forgetting to add in the information about the passport. The claimant then stated that in July 2009 another interpreter advised him that he should amend his Personal Information Form and add in the information that he has a genuine Chinese passport. The claimant was asked why he failed to identify the serial number, date of issue and date of expiry of his passport. He stated that he could not get the information because he was afraid to have the passport sent in the mail. The claimant was asked why he simply did not telephone his parents and ask them for the information over the telephone. The claimant failed to respond to the question and sat in silence. The Panel rejects the claimant's explanations for the inconsistency between his oral evidence and his Personal Information Form regarding the existence of a passport and birth certificate in China. The Panel makes this finding given the claimant's lack of a reasonable explanation. The Panel finds on a balance of probabilities that it is implausible that two interpreters would provide not just interpretation to the claimant but advice regarding his identity documents and that he would be advised that such documents would not be necessary for the hearing. The claimant provided no motive or persuasive explanation for why the interpreters would provide false information on the claimant's Personal Information Form.

Furthermore, although the claimant testified that he was aware that personal identity would be an issue in the hearing, he failed to provide a reasonable explanation why he would not have picked up his telephone and asked his parents for the details of his passport and also have asked them to forward the passport and birth certificate. As stated earlier, the claimant is represented by qualified Counsel and the claimant had over two years to obtain the documentation from China.

Finally, at the commencement of the hearing, the claimant having reviewed his Personal Information Form, declared that the entire contents of the document were completely interpreted to him before he signed the form and that as of the date of the hearing, the document was complete, true and correct. The claimant was given the opportunity to explain why, after declaring that the document was complete, true and correct to the Panel, that the claimant later in the hearing indicated that the information contained in questions 13 and 14 and 22 of the form was incorrect. The claimant provided the Panel with no reasonable explanation, except to place blame on whoever assisted him in completing the form. The Panel rejects this explanation as it fails to provide a reasonable explanation for the inconsistencies in the claimant's evidence. Request for Time to Obtain Chinese Birth Certificate and Passport

During the latter part of the initial sitting of the hearing, the claimant advised the Panel that now that he was aware of the great importance of the documents to the Panel, he could provide by way of facsimile, a copy of both his Chinese birth certificate and his Chinese passport "over night" to the Panel. The claimant then stated that he could also provide by way of courier, his genuine original Chinese birth certificate and genuine original Chinese passport to his Counsel by February 2, 2010. The Counsel indicated that he could provide the genuine original Chinese birth certificate and genuine original Chinese passport the Panel by February 3, 2010.

Given the importance of the identity documents to the outcome of the hearing, the Panel decided to give the claimant the benefit of the doubt and decided to adjourn the proceedings to allow the claimant to provide both his genuine original Chinese birth certificate and genuine original Chinese passport in support of his claim to be a national of the People's Republic of China. The Panel advised the claimant that he did not need to fax the documents "over night" as he had promised, but directed him to fax them to his Counsel by January 21, 2010 (two days following the hearing) and Counsel agreed to submit the faxes to the Panel by January 22, 2010. The Panel directed the claimant to provide the genuine, original documents to his Counsel by February 2, 2010, allowing two weeks for the documents to be couriered. Counsel agreed to submit the documents to the Panel by February 3, 2010. Both the Panel and the claimant's Counsel gave clear and specific directions to the claimant regarding the method that was going to be used to transport the documents to the Panel and also the specific dates that the documents would be provided. The claimant assured both the Panel and Counsel that he was aware of the timelines and the mode of transportation of the documents. The claimant clearly stated that he would be able to have the documents faxed to his Counsel and then have the originals couriered to Canada. The Panel explained clearly to the claimant that it was important to adhere to the timelines and that if he did not, the Panel may draw a negative inference in regard to credibility because the claimant had assured the Panel that the documents exist, and are readily available in China.

The claimant failed to provide either the fax of his Chinese passport or birth certificate to his Counsel by January 21, 2010 or to the Panel by January 22, 2010. The claimant failed to provide his original genuine Chinese passport or birth certificate to his Counsel by February 2, 2010 or the Panel on February 3, 2010. On March 17, 2010, seven and a half weeks after the faxed copy of the documents was due, and six weeks after the original documents were due, the Panel was given a Chinese birth certificate alleged to be the claimant's original birth certificate and a photocopy of one page of a passport, alleged to be that of the claimant's. Upon receipt of the documents, no explanation was provided regarding the late disclosure of the documents, nor any explanation for why the documents were not the exact documents requested by and promised to the Panel by both the claimant and Counsel.
The hearing reconvened on April 28, 2010. By the second sitting, the claimant's complete original Chinese passport was still not provided to the Panel.

The claimant was asked why he had not complied with the instructions of the Panel and his Counsel by not providing a faxed copy of his Chinese passport and Chinese birth certificate by January 19, 2010. He was also asked why he failed to provide the originals by way of courier by February 2, 2010. The claimant initially responded that his parents did not fax the documents to his Counsel because there are no fax machines in his village or local area. It was noted that the area in which the claimant comes from, Guangzhou City, is the capital city of Guangdong province and is the most populous city in the province of Guangdong province, with a population in the several millions in both the urban area and the rural areas.12 The claimant was given the opportunity to explain how plausibility given the demographics and nature of Guangzhou City it was plausible that his parents would be unable to find a facsimile machine, especially when they were live in the capital of the province, the claimant suggested that it was because his father is an unsophisticated person who was unable to fax documents. When asked why another family member, such as his twenty-one year old sister who he said attends high school in Guangzhou, could not fax the documents to him, he responded that she "can't be bothered" to help him because she does not care enough about his circumstances to help him in his manner. The claimant was asked if he had advised his father of the importance of faxing the documents as quickly as possible because they were needed for his refugee claim, and he responded in the affirmative. The claimant stated that he was unable to provide any corroborating documentary evidence to support his assertion that there are no fax machines in his area of China.

The Panel asked the claimant why he had previously told the Panel that he could easily fax the documents overnight, if there are no fax machines in his community in Guangzhou city and he provided no explanation, except to state that he did not know that there would be a problem locating a fax machine. The Panel rejects this explanation and draws a negative inference in regard to credibility given the implausible explanation given by the claimant that in an area as large and populous as Guangzhou City, his family was unable to find a facsimile machine to fax the claimant's birth certificate and passport. It is a reasonable expectation that even the claimant's sister who attends high school would have access to a facsimile machine and would have the ability to fax the documents.

The claimant said that because his parents could not locate a fax machine they mailed the birth certificate and passport by regular mail. The claimant was asked if he had the original envelope which the documents arrived in and he said that he "threw the envelope away" because he did not think it was important. The claimant stated that the passport never arrived in Canada because it was seized by the Chinese postal workers after they had asked his father what was in the envelope and his father had responded that it was the claimant's "passport and he was ending it to Canada". The claimant said that the birth certificate was in another envelope and that his father was never questioned about that envelope because he mailed it from another location.

The claimant failed to provide the Panel with a Notice of Seizure from the postal authorities in regard to the seizure of his passport and he was given the opportunity to explain why he did not have a seizure notice, given that he provided such a document for his Resident Identity Card. The claimant responded that he did not know why no seizure notice was issued but suggested that perhaps a different post office would have different rules for the issuance of such documents.

The Panel draws a negative inference in regard to credibility given the claimant's assertion that he could easily fax the documents "overnight" and easily obtain the original documents within days of the hearing and then his inability or unwillingness to do so. During the first sitting, the Panel was very clear in her oral direction to the claimant that the documents must be received on time and in complete. The claimant failed to produce the birth certificate on time and the passport, when received, was only a one page photocopy.

With respect to the assessment of the documents, section 106 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act states: The Refugee Protection Division must take into account, with respect to the credibility of a claimant, whether the claimant possesses acceptable documentation establishing identity, and if not, whether they have provided a reasonable explanation for the lack of documentation or have taken reasonable steps to obtain the documentation.

Rule 7 of the Refugee Protection Division Rules states: The claimant must provide acceptable documents establishing identity and other elements of the claim. A claimant who does not provide acceptable documents must explain why they were not provided and what steps were taken to obtain them.

In assessing the authenticity of the claimant's documents, the Panel is guided by the Federal Court decision in Sertkaya13 which asserts that it is open for the Immigration and Refugee Board to consider the authenticity of documentary evidence, and the ability of the claimant to obtain and use fraudulent documents. The Panel is also mindful of the Federal Court decision in Rasheed,14 which asserts that the basic rule in Canadian law is that foreign documents (whether they establish the identity or not of a claimant) purporting to be issued by a competent foreign public official should be accepted as evidence of their content unless the Immigration and Refugee Board has some valid reason to doubt their authenticity. Notice of Seizure of Resident Identity Card

The claimant presented a notice of Seizure of Resident Identity Card in support of his identity as a national of the People's Republic of China. As explained earlier, the Panel draws a negative inference in regard to the unreasonable and implausible explanation provided by the claimant for the contradiction between his oral testimony and the documentary evidence he provided and draws a negative inference in regard to credibility and the claimant's identity as a Chinese national. Birth Certificate

The Birth certificate provided to the Panel15 alleged by the claimant to be his original genuine birth certificate, lacks information that according to country conditions documents, genuine Chinese birth certificates contain. Birth certificates normally include a registration number, and the race, and the Resident Identity Card numbers and nationality of parents.16 Given this discrepancy between what information a Chinese birth certificate normally contains and the omission of this information from the birth certificate provided by the claimant and in the context of the claimant's inability or unwillingness to provide the birth certificate copy on January 21, 2010 and the original on February 2, 2010, and given that the claimant failed to declare that he had a birth certificate in his Personal Information Form, even after amending his Personal Information Form on January 19, 2010 and in the context of negative credibility findings made, the Panel finds on a balance of probabilities that the birth certificate is a fraudulent document. Fraudulent Chinese documents are known to be easily obtained in China.17 The Claimant's Passport
The passport provided to the Panel on March 17, 2010 consisted of only a photocopy of one page of the passport.

The Panel draws a negative inference in regard to credibility and the claimant's identity as a nation of the China given his inability to provide not even a complete photocopy of the original passport in the timeline he said he could meet, given that he testified that his genuine passport was with his parents in China.

The Panel notes that the claimant filed his claim for refugee protection on October 17, 2007 and at that time he noted that he was represented by an immigration consultant Daniel Zhang.18 Also when the he completed his Personal Information Form on December 24, 2007, the claimant indicated that he was represented by the same Counsel who represented him at the hearing.19 The claimant had more than two years to obtain both his passport and birth certificate prior to the first sitting of the hearing and he failed to do so. The Panel draws a negative inference in regard to the claimant's credibility and his identity as a national of China given the claimant's failure to provide these documents to the Panel. The Claimant's Chinese Household Registry
A Household Register was submitted in support of the claimant's identity.20

The Household Register submitted is on its face, questionable as to its authenticity. The Chinese household registry lacks information that according to country conditions documents, genuine Chinese household registries contain. Chinese household registry normally includes the national's employment occupation,21 but in the instant case, the occupation is left blank. Given this discrepancy between what information a Chinese household registry normally contains and the omission of this information from the Chinese household registry provided, and in the context of the negative credibility findings previously made, the Panel finds on a balance of probabilities that the household registry provided to the Panel is a fraudulent document.

In June 9, 2009 correspondence, a professor of international affairs at the Georgia Institute of Technology, who has published on the hukou system in China, stated that both hukou forgery and acquiring a genuine hukou by fraudulent means "have been observed for a long time" in China.22

The Panel wanted to give the claimant the opportunity to demonstrate his knowledge of his Household Registry and the Hukou system in China in order to allow him to offer his subjective knowledge in support of his allegation that he is a Chinese national. The claimant stated in his oral testimony that the Household Registry was not as important as the Chinese birth certificate and passport and he was asked to explain why he did not think the household registry was an important document. The claimant initially responded that the Chinese household registry does not identify people. He then changed his testimony and stated that the household registry does not identify people by their photographs and that is the reason he thinks his household registry was not seized by Chinese postal officials. The claimant was given the opportunity to explain his statements given that the household registry does clearly identify people and provides a great deal of written information about Chinese citizens including their rural or urban designation, resident identity card, address, family composition, occupation, sex, place of birth, ethnic group, marital status, blood type, religion, height and other information23 but he failed to provide an explanation for his apparent lack of knowledge about the information contained in the household registry.

The claimant was given the opportunity to describe the utility of the household registry. The claimant responded that it confirmed that he lived in the country of China but "not much other use". When asked if it was used for anything else, the claimant responded in the negative. However it was pointed out to the claimant that the household registry has many important uses in China, including its main use of identifying rural and urban citizens, resource distribution, migration control and the management of people, including access to education and the eligibility for social services, unemployment or social welfare support.24 When asked why he had no idea of the uses of the household registry, including the requirement to show the document when registering for school, the claimant stated that "he was not clear". The claimant then said that because his parents used the household registry, he was unaware of its uses. However the Panel noted that the claimant was an adult of twenty-four years of age when he left China and as an adult, having grown up in China, finds it is unreasonable that the claimant would have absolutely no knowledge of the many uses of the household registry in China. The Panel draws a negative inference in regard to credibility and the claimant's identity as a national of China given his extremely limited knowledge of the household registry system in China. Furthermore the Panel finds on a balance of probabilities, that given the claimant's inability to provide any explanation for the lack of his occupation noted on the Household Registry combined with his absolute lack of knowledge regarding the household registry, and in the context of negative credibility findings made, that it cannot trust the validity of the Household Registry. For this reason, the Panel finds on a balance of probabilities that the Household Register is not an authentic identity document.

In making this determination there is no obligation on the Panel to submit the Household Registry to the Royal Canadian Mounted Police for forensic testing. In the Federal Court decision of Jin,25 Mr. Justice Barnes stated: While it is correct that the Board is not itself an expert in the field of forensic analysis, it also has no duty to submit suspect documents for expert assessment provided that there is sufficient evidence before it to cast doubt upon their authenticity.

Furthermore, the Federal Court has said that if the Immigration and Refugee Board has sufficient evidence that the claimant's identity has not been established, that the Immigration and Refugee Board is under no obligation to send further identity documents for forensic analysis.26

In conclusion, given that the documentation of the country conditions27obtained from independent sources indicate that there is a flourishing trade of fraudulent identity documents used by refugee claimants, the Panel therefore finds, on a balance of probabilities, and in the context of negative credibility findings made, that the claimant's Household Registry and Birth certificate cannot be relied upon as genuine. SUMMATION:

The Panel is guided by Justice Layden-Stevenson in the Federal Court decision of Lin28 and understands the obligation of the Panel to consider the totality of the evidence before it when considering the issue of identity. The Panel is guided by this Federal Court decision, and having considered the totality of the evidence before it, including Counsel's post hearing final written submissions, relevant documents, statutory provisions and case law, including the oral evidence provided by the claimant during the hearing, the Panel finds that on a balance of probabilities that the claimant has failed to produce sufficient credible documents and evidence to establish his identity as a national of the People's Republic of China, nor has he satisfactorily explained why such evidence was not provided. Given the many inconsistencies, contradictions and implausibilities that were not reasonably explained by the claimant, the Panel finds on a balance of probabilities that the claimant is not a credible witness in regard to his identity as a national of the People's Republic of China.

Furthermore, the claimant has not met the requirements of section 106 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act and Rule 7 of the Refugee Protection Division Rules, and has knowingly submitted false documents. Accordingly, the Panel finds that the claimant is not a credible witness.

In Ibnmogdad29 Justice Tremblay-Lamer commented that, The matter of foreign documents is not an area where the tribunal could claim particular knowledge (Ramalingam). However, there is no duty on the tribunal to obtain an expert report where there is sufficient evidence to cast doubt on their authenticity (Culinescu, Kashif). In this case, the documents speak for themselves. The tribunal concluded that by submitting identity documents that were clearly not authentic the applicant demonstrated that he was not a witness to be trusted. This conclusion is consistent with s. 106 of IRPA. Once it concluded the identity had not been established it was not necessary for the Board to analyze the evidence any further (Husein).

The Panel finds that the claimant has failed to establish his identity as a national of the People's Republic of China. Therefore there is no need for further analysis of the claimant's allegations, given that it matters not, pursuant to section 106 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, whether the claimant is a practicing Christian. Given that the claimant has not established his personal identity, the Panel needs not to go on to assess the merits of his claim.

Having found that the claimant is not a citizen of the People's Republic of China and the totality of the evidence, the Panel finds that there is not a serious possibility that the claimant would be persecuted in the People's Republic of China on any Convention ground, nor that there exist substantial grounds to believe that the claimant would be subjected personally to a danger of torture, nor that he will be subjected personally to a risk to his life or to cruel and unusual treatment or punishment in the People's Republic of China.

The Panel finds that the claimant is neither a Convention refugee nor is he a person in need of protection. The Refugee Protection Division therefore rejects his claim. (signed) "Cynthia L.
